utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wished to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours and thank you. Could I ask that I do this in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Banbury.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You found the right courtroom, I see. A different one. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will continue with the same document that we had before us yesterday, Mr. Banbury. Could we now please show in e-court P764 and could we look at paragraph 3(a) -- rather, paragraph 4.3. If you recall, sir, yesterday we discussed a document that was drafted as a summary of the talks that you attended, the talks on the 21st of July, 1994, and we talked about the issues that were broached by General Mladic at that meeting. Now I would like you to take a look at paragraph (e) which reads -- I don't know if you can see it before you. It's point (e) where it says that Mladic stated that the Serbs were very upset over the reduction in food deliveries by UNHCR to the Serb side. He said that the Serbs now had great difficulty bringing in food, medical supplies, fuel, and spare parts for the motor transport industry which was creating extreme economic hardship for the Serb people. I'd just like to ask you this: From what you knew about the situation on the ground, the situation in which the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina found itself, was that in fact in accordance with what you were told by General Mladic at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly am aware that throughout the conflict many Serb civilians suffered all different kinds of deprivations including in the humanitarian sphere, access to enough food, access to heating in winter, so I know that civilians throughout Bosnia, regardless of their national origin, really suffered from the impact of the war on a humanitarian level. In terms of the other issues raised in that paragraph such as degradation of roads, I'm less aware of that, though. It was an issue that I know UNPROFOR engineers worked on a lot. We had armoured personnel carriers, some of them tracked that certainly impacted roads. In terms of industrial or agricultural production of any of the sides, that was not something that UNPROFOR spent much attention on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like you to take a look at paragraph (e)of your summary of this meeting where you paraphrased the words of General Mladic that he insisted on the Serb continuing check the convoys in detail, and he requested, in particular, equipment for checking the presence of explosives so that these controls could be carried out more easily. He said that he had already promised that by Generals Briquemont and Morillon. My first question is: Do you have any knowledge of that, that before you arrived in talks with Generals Briquemont and Morillon that such a possibility was envisaged?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any personal knowledge of anything that General Briquemont or Morillon may have pledged to General Mladic in this regard, though I do know that it was a somewhat common practice for UN representations to be later on misrepresented by the -- in particular the Bosnian Serb leadership. What we had said we would do was often mischaracterised later in a different context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're referring to a section, capital A. Where is it exactly what you are referring to? Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps there was a problem with interpretation. I mentioned point 3(e) under freedom -- and the title is "freedom of movement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is (g) rather than (e). That may have caused the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (g) (i).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've found it meanwhile. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I wanted to ask you about this message of yours is this: You said that Mladic insisted that the Serbs would continue to closely examine our convoys. In the agreement on the movement of convoys, was the possibility envisaged that the documents and the goods that are being transported can be cross checked?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, which particular agreement are you referring to? We had many different arrangements over the course of time on convoy movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about July 1994 then. At that time, the Serb side or the federation side in the event that convoys went through the territories under their controls, did they have the ability to actually cross-reference the documents, the accompanying documents, and the goods that are being transported on those trucks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you said did they have the ability. Your previous question was about agreement. Did you mean practical possibilities to do or whether they were entitled under whatever kind of agreement? If it is the latter, you should clearly indicate which agreement you're referring to. If it's the former, then please make that clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So first I'll ask you - thank you. Thank you, Your Honours - first, I'll ask you were they entitled to do these checks?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view no party was entitled to conduct such checks as matter of the -- or based on the legal status of UNPROFOR and the rights given to us by the Security Council. Having said that, UNPROFOR often did enter into arrangements, in particular with the Bosnian Serb side as a very practical matter to get our convoys through. Otherwise, they could not -- the Bosnian Serbs would not let them pass. So while they were not entitled to legally speaking, we nonetheless agreed to arrangements that let them do certain cross-checking between the documents we submitted and the checks of the convoys on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Banbury. Did the federation side have similar entitlements? I think that was the question that was put by Mr. Stojanovic, whether the federation did have this cross-checking of goods with consignments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The arrangements with the federation were always very different, and we never had these kinds of difficulties with transport of our goods, our personnel, humanitarian supplies, convoys, et cetera, with the federation. The legal rights of UNPROFOR, of course, were the same, but as a practicality matter we were not -- it was not necessary for us to enter into those kinds of arrangements with the federation or either of the two component parts of the federation because they did not place the same kinds of restrictions on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will conclude with one last question about the movement of convoys. Would you agree that these convoys that were inspected by the Republika Srpska authorities were convoys the destination of which was the area in the territory of the federation and specifically the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on -- on which convoys you're referring to. We had convoys moving on a daily basis or sometimes it wasn't even a convoy. It could have been a single passenger vehicle with a couple civil affairs officers, but the destination in principle was immaterial. It's a United Nations convoy. Secondly, the destination was either an UNPROFOR establishment, wherever it was located, it was to an UNPROFOR military base or an UNPROFOR office or an UNPROFOR civilian police office, or it was a humanitarian assistance destination, a warehouse, a distribution point for humanitarian assistance. Geographically where it was located for the UN, I think, was much less material but oftentimes it was into the eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of any case where the convoys meant for Republika Srpska crossed over the territory of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that must have happened on a very regular basis given our supply lines and the humanitarian supply lines coming up from the coast. I'm sure there must have been on a very regular basis convoys, whether it was humanitarian or UNPROFOR resupply or simply UNPROFOR personnel who went from federation-controlled area to Serb-controlled area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now take a look at paragraph 5 of this document. Here, the way I read it, in your summary you mention your own words, what you said to General Mladic on that occasion relating to the release of prisoners and detainees. If I read -- am reading this correctly, and that's why I'm asking you, on that occasion you said to Mr. Mladic that you could understand -- that you understood what he was talking about and that you were determined -- it to affect an unconditional release of all prisoners and detainees in co-operation with the ICRC. Now, I'm asking you this: What -- because you mentioned what the possible problem might be. So what I would like to know is: Did you have any information at any point in time it actually did happen that an unconditional release of all prisoners and detainees materialised as General Mladic mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should first clarify that the I pronoun in this paragraph refers to Mr. Andreev and not myself. Though I drafted the document, it's signed by and sent by Mr. Andreev. So it's he who made that representation to General Mladic and not myself. In terms of the specific answer to your question, I do not believe that there was ever any unconditional release of or exchange of prisoners of war between the sides during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now conclude with paragraph 9 in this document. Paragraph 9 which completes the message and it stresses, among other things, the following: We have to avoid a situation in which the Serbs believe that UNPROFOR is biased, in favour of one of the parties in the conflict. Therefore, we have to take advantage of opportunities to co-operate with Serbs in the field with regard to issues such as taking rubbish away, and so on, so that the level of trust between the Serbs and UNPROFOR can be raised. What is the reason for which the conclusion is that you have to avoid a situation in which in which the Serbs might believe that UNPROFOR is biased?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This issue was a dominant theme throughout my time in Bosnia, and it -- it was at the basis of the relationship between the Bosnian Serbs and UNPROFOR, and I know that UNPROFOR worked extremely hard to do its job in a fair and unbiased and impartial manner putting first the needs of the civilian population in Bosnian. Sometimes that worked to the advantage of one party, sometimes to the advantage of another, hopefully always to the advantage of the civilians. But General Mladic and some of his colleagues in Pale worked very hard to pressure UNPROFOR to do more -- to act in a way that would favour them more and to make us feel like we were biased or make us feel guilty or make us feel like we were doing something wrong and constantly pointing out areas where they thought we had failed or accusing us of misbehaviour in order to precisely get the reaction or response from UNPROFOR that is reflected in that document, where we sought to bend over backwards to show that we were not biased so we would go to extra lengths, whether it was collecting garbage in towns or any other number of ways to try and demonstrate that we were not biased, so that we could get other things that were important to us, particularly related to protection of -- or assistance to civilian populations, and I think that this is -- it's a very good example of that extremely unfortunate dynamic in the relationship between the Bosnian Serb leadership and the UNPROFOR leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now show you another document that -- I would like us to have P764 before us, and please focus on one of the sentences that General Mladic said according to this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 6 (a), Your Honours, in this document. Could we please have a look at it. Here it says that, among other things, Mladic also mentioned the issue of the alleged bad relationship with the Serbs in towns under Bosniak control; for example, Sarajevo, Tuzla, Travnik, and Busovaca and Konjic. Could we now see 1D00711, and then I'll put some questions to you about these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, according to the information you have, sir, during that period of time in 1994, were there still Serbs living there, and did you have any information on what the relationship was with the Serbian population in the towns mentioned by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were Serbs living in those towns, but sorry, I didn't understand the second part of your question about the relationship, the relationship between those Serb populations and UNPROFOR or the federation authorities? I'm sorry, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The relationship between the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the previous document. P764. You asked for paragraph 6(a), and it was on the screen but it disappeared.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6(a). 6(a), thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question concerned this relationship, this attitude of the federation authorities with regard to the Serbian population in the towns that were referred to.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your -- your question is on the federation authorities, and I believe that as a political matter, the federation authorities had a very strong commitment to the multi-ethnicity of the federation. They -- they did it for perhaps a variety of reasons, but nonetheless they sought very hard to maintain the multi-ethnic character of not only Sarajevo but the federation as a whole, and we -- I saw that in -- in any number of ways. So that was the federation authority official policy. No doubt there were cases of individual Serbs or Serb families or Serb communities living in different parts of the federation who were suffering various kinds of deprivations including humanitarian. That being said, the Muslim or Croat family living next door to them was usually suffering the exact same kinds of humanitarian deprivations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that people moved towards territory under the control of the army that was composed of their own ethnicity? Serbs moved towards Republika Srpska, the Muslims moved toward territory under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croats moved toward territory under the control of the HVO. Is that how this operated?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general matter, yes, I would certainly agree with that characterisation, though there were absolutely important exceptions to that general trend, especially in Sarajevo, less so in perhaps rural areas or smaller cities, but Sarajevo throughout the conflict did maintain in its society, its commercial aspects, its way of life and even in the government, a multi-ethnic dimension. And I, for instance, had Serb friends living in Sarajevo who absolutely refused to consider leaving the city during the war. So as a general trend, yes, but important exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we see 1D711 in e-court again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 1st of October, 1992, drafted at the request of the ICRC after a meeting in Geneva. Let's have a look at page 2 both in the English and the B/C/S version. At the meeting it was proposed under 1 that civilians who desired to temporarily leave the territory controlled by one of the parties to reach the territory controlled by another party should be entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's page 2 of document 1D711, paragraph 1 of the conclusion. After the title the underside -- under the heading, in fact, the undersigned submit the following recommendations to the deliberation of the internation conference on former Yugoslavia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any information about the fact that as early as 1992 such a proposal was made concerning the possibility for civilians to leave the territory under the control of one of the parties and move over to territory under the control of one of the other parties?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this particular document that was written a long time before I arrived in Bosnia and just a few months after the conflict began, but I would say it's -- and I used to work for UNHCR as well. It's a fundamental principle for the United Nations that people should be allowed free movement and should not be held prisoner or should not be restrained from free movement whether for travel purposes or to relocate, to live somewhere else. So that is certainly a principle that the United Nations, the one contained in paragraph 1, certainly a principle that the United Nations would subscribe to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 it says that civilians should be able to leave in an organised manner under international supervision and, if necessary, protection. Its security -- or their security will be guaranteed by each party in the territory it controls. Did you have any information about the fact that this is how during that difficult wartime period an attempt was made to ensure that the population could move around freely?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many efforts to ensure the security of people who wished to leave from one area and move to other whether by UNPROFOR or the ICRC. So this is consistent with certainly efforts by different international organisations. I know that there were many, many times where it was not possible for the UN to ensure that this particular -- the principles in this particular paragraph were respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D711 receives number D192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D192 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of the fact that the policies of one of the warring factions included calling on the people that were the majority in the territory under their control and appealing to them to move out of territory under the control of the opposing faction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have one specific warring faction in mind, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, but I will in relation to the next document that I will be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm a little confused by the question in re-reading the transcript. I wonder if -- I think I understand the question, but maybe in the transcript the way it's worded it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first invite Mr. Stojanovic to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try -- I apologise if it was very general. I'll try and be more specific. At any point in time did you have any information according to which the warring factions, the ABiH and the federation authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, appeal to the Bosniak and Croatian population to move to territory under their control and vice versa? Did you have any information according to which the authorities in Republika Srpska appealed to the Serbian population to move to territory under their control and to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that -- well, it's certainly the case that the question of population residences of different groups, minority, majority, population movements were difficult and dominant issues throughout the conflict, and many things were said by many people formally and informally during the course of the conflict. I don't know what the official stated policy by the highest authorities of the different factions were with respect to the population movements. I -- well, on the federation side, I know that they -- they wanted to certainly maintain the multi-ethnic character of the federation as I mentioned before. I believe they also for various reasons wanted to maintain the -- maintain minority populations in Serb-controlled areas. I believe the Bosnian Serbs were much more interested in having a mono-ethnic character to the land they controlled, and they associated the presence of Serbs in an area with sovereignty over the land, and I've heard senior Bosnian Serb officials say very clearly that where a Serb boot rests that will be Serb land. Whether that's the official policy or position, it's I think a little hard to -- for me to say, but that was my understanding of the positions of the different sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 1D709. Sir, it's because of this document that I, in fact, put this question to you -- or in relation to this document that I put this question to you, because I think we'll be able to comment on it if we bear in mind the date when this document was drafted. It was drafted by the Party of Democratic Action in Trebinje on the 20th of January, 1993. The title of the document is "instructions concerning moving out from Trebinje," signed by the then SDA secretary, Hasan Cengic. And paragraph 1 says: Through activists we should animate all Muslims, especially prominent and wealthy ones so that they leave Trebinje as soon as possible and move to Montenegro. Paragraph 2 suggests what should be done with property. And paragraph 3 says: Do not refrain from exerting pressure and even using force against those Muslims who fail to respect this order. First of all, would we agree that in 1993, Trebinje was under the control of the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes my recollection of which town was under the control of which party or faction at a given time isn't perfect at this stage, but I certainly accept that that is very likely the case, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Secondly, could we agree that the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, was the most prominent political organisation, the strongest political organisation that held power, in fact, in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January 1993, there was no federation yet, but the SDA was certainly the most powerful political party in the territory controlled by the government or the ARBiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And could we agree that this document drafted by the secretary of that party appeals to the Muslims and encourages them to leave Trebinje. It says that force could be applied or should be applied against those who fail to respect this order. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the English translation that I have here says, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, talking about English translation, I don't know whether it is original but the English language now and then strikes me as not the best, perhaps. Do you know whether this -- for example, this heading at the top is not translated. Where does this translation come from? Is it an official translation, or has it been distributed at the time in two languages, which is also of course possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can't answer that question with certainty, but I know where I obtained it from. I obtained it from the Karadzic case, but at this point in time I can't tell you who did the translation, but I could check up on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please inform us. Could the parties pay attention. Could they have a look at the English version and see whether it needs to be reviewed or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will conclude with another sentence from this document. Mr. Banbury, please have a look at paragraph 5 where it says: All your property -- or you will be reimbursed for all your property when we achieve our goal and we'll know how to value your sacrifice, and this is what the Muslims throughout the world expect of you. Respectfully "selamu alejkum" SDA secretary, Hasan Cengic. During your stay from April up until the summer of 1995, April 1994 to the summer of 1995, during that period of time did you learn anything about the fact that the parallel policies of the SDA were, in fact, an attempt to move the Muslim population out of territory that was under the control of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have the impression that the SDA sought to manipulate population issues, including the Muslim population of Bosnia in ways that it perceived as favourable to it, and while I certainly was not aware of this document, the approach taken in it is absolutely reprehensible and one that UNPROFOR would have sought to fight against, and we consistently did confront extremely difficult population issues and always sought to protect the rights of civilian populations. That being said, we would do that working with the official authorities of the different factions. In the case of the Bosnian government, it would be the government and not the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, your reference to paragraph 5 must have been a reference to the B/C/S version, because the English version has no paragraph 5. There seems to be another mistake there, an additional reason to have the translation reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I suggest that 1D709 be marked for identification at this point in time, and we'll try to obtain an official translation and tender that into evidence when it is provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D709 receives number D193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D193 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it might be time to have a break as has been suggested to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly is time for a break. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, Mr. Groome, there was a motion yesterday for the Theunens report, the 30 days to be counted on from the refiling of the Theunens report. You've seen that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I haven't yet, Your Honour, but I was familiar with some e-mail correspondence that preceded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any -- is there any final disagreement because the motion says at a certain moment we propose to the Prosecution but we didn't receive a response. Is there any problem with starting the 30 days when the new report is filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's going to be our position to oppose that, Your Honour, because the Chamber's asked us to redact material and we believe that the issues relevant to the response are all in the table at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for your -- we'll wait for your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When can we that approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can tell you at the next break, Your Honour, I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Banbury. Mr. Stojanovic will continue his cross-examination. Mr. Stojanovic, could you give us any idea as far as time is concerned? Any more precise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just as we said yesterday, I believe that I will be done after the second session, these two sessions; in other words, another two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we would have one session left. I need at the end of this session I need two or three minutes of the time of the parties for a matter to be dealt with in private session. But let's first start the continued cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, I would like again to refer you to your statement, P874, and briefly to paragraph 44 of your statement. Among other things there it is stated and this is on the 28th of August, 1994 -- among other things it says there that the Bosnian government had threatened to cut off the supply into the entire country as well as the 30 per cent diverted to the FRY. Now, I would just like to ask you this: When you said that, what did you mean? In what way or how was it that the Bosnian government could cut off the supply of gas to the entire country and the 30 per cent to the FRY? Technically speaking or physically, how was that possible?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a technical expert on this matter at all, but I do know that because of the particular way the natural gas delivery infrastructure system was built in the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that the gas came or some of -- a large portion of the gas for Bosnia and some even for the other parts of the FRY came into Sarajevo and then in -- I guess some kind of large pipeline and then was distributed to out in smaller ways to different parts of Bosnia and the FRY, which did create a very interesting and in some ways I'd say helpful dynamic, because each party depended upon the other to have natural gas. So that is a very general nontechnical, nonexpert description of what my understanding of the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So have I understood this correctly: Your understanding of this threat by the Bosnia-Herzegovina government, was it in fact something that could be accomplished, that could be effected? Is that how you understood the -- this distribution line?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I will not insist on this any longer. Now let us take a look together at paragraph 54 of your statement. Do you have it before you? Could we please also show it in e-court. Paragraph 54. So let me give you some context. These are developments of September 1994 which can be seen from the previous page of your statement. So I'd just like to ask you this: Do you remember that at some point in time the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia authorities or government in fact introduced economic sanctions on the Drina River --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- to the -- to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 54, you talk about describing Slobodan Milosevic. You talk about his policies. Up until then, how many times did you have occasion to meet with and hear the positions of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, because I don't know the date of this -- that is encapsulated in this paragraph. If -- in the previous paragraph, paragraph 53, refers to August 1994. If -- and I see in paragraph 56 it's September 1994. So if we are talking about the period of summer of 1994, I had not at that time ever met President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 54 here, as far as I can see, this relates to late August. You say here that you thought that Slobodan Milosevic had a great influence on the Bosnian Serbs, including Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. And then you say there was a mutual desire also to have close ties between the FRY and the RS, two entities with symbolic barriers between them to facilitate the ready exchange of people, goods and services. As time progressed, their interests became evermore divergent and as that happened Milosevic's ability to impose his will diminished. My question is this: What did you base this conclusion on?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps first just a technical correction. In my paragraph I referred to two entities with low barriers between them and in the translation it said with symbolic barriers between them. But to answer your question, sir, I based this conclusion on -- it's an analysis based on an overall assessment or effort to understand what was happening in Bosnia and beyond, drawing on all available resources, conversations that I happened to be present for between senior UNPROFOR officials and Bosnian Serb leaders, reports from other parts of UNPROFOR, a lot on the press reporting from the time, including Bosnian Serb and FRY press reporting. So it was an overall assessment based on all the material I had available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on during your the later months of your stay in the area of the former Yugoslavia, this divergent tendency after the sanctions were imposed on Republika Srpska by the FRY, did this divergence actually continue? Did it grow wider?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was my impression that the divergence did grow wider, but that was especially true in the relationship between the political forces and, in particular, President Milosevic and Dr. Karadzic and also perhaps in the commercial area, the movement of goods, commercial goods, across the Drina or from FRY to the -- to the Republika Srpska. But I think the relationship between the Yugoslav Army and the Bosnian Serb Army and the leadership of the Bosnian Serb Army, General Mladic, and President Milosevic and General Perisic, remained much closer than the differences in the political and commercial area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get back to that a little later when we speak about a meeting that you mention a little later in your statement, but for now let us take a look at paragraph 65 of your statement. Mr. Banbury, do you remember that there was a continuing problem of the Sarajevo airport and its use, because in paragraph 65, you say that it was another frequent topic.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The issue of Sarajevo airport, the ability for the UN to operate in and out of it was a continuing problem for UNPROFOR during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that the BH Army, too, at -- in some moments in fact made it impossible for the airport to be used because they opened fire on the airport facilities?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not personally aware of any time that the Bosnian Army shut down the airport because of military actions it took. There were times where UNPROFOR planes were shot and it was impossible to determine the origin of the firing, so I do not rule out the possibility that our operations at the airport were impacted by Bosnian Army activity. But I have no knowledge that -- of a single incident where the Bosnian Army shot at our planes. On the contrary, we know for a fact that there were many, many instances where the Bosnian Serb forces shut down UN operations at the airport either by targeting our aircraft or simply by telling us that they could not guarantee the safety of our aircraft which by definition, whenever they told us that we would cease flying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now have 1D716 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, this document is dated the 13th of August, 1994. That's the period that we're discussing right now. It is sent by Brigadier-General van Baal to Brigadier-General Jovan Divjak, deputy commander of the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, first of all, do you know or does the name Brigadier-General van Baal mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally know General van Baal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know General Jovan Divjak?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes, I have met General Divjak. I knew General van Baal rather well and worked frequently with him. General Divjak I only met on a small number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this document, Mr. Baal says - I'll be brief - that in close to this letter, he also sends a report by the commander of the airport regarding the opening of fire on the 18th of August. And in paragraph 2 it says it turns out again that three bullets were fired from the area under the control of the BH Army, which led to the air-lift being cut off or the suspension of air-lifts, and in fact this was -- in essence this was an irrational act. Does this help refresh your memory that there were incidents as I suggested, incidents caused by the BH Army that led to occasional suspensions of air-lifts?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall this particular incident, but I have no reason to -- to doubt it, and as I said, I was -- I accept the possibility that there were -- was firing by the Army of the BiH that impacted airport operations. So I -- while I'm not familiar with this incident, I accept the letter from General van Baal and if there's a report from the airport commander that says it, the UN airport commander, then I would accept that as being the -- what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence. That's D716, 1D716. That's its 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D716 receives number D194, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, therefore admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now could we see 1D720 in e-court, please. 1D720.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We see that the situation there is similar. I would just like to show you this document again. It's authored by General van Baal addressed to General Jovan Divjak, and this time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the witness said that he -- that UN aircraft were fired at, that it was impossible to -- at least for this witness and he has no knowledge of the origin of fire, therefore to put him to him other examples where he says he doesn't know, unless, Witness, you would change -- have changed your mind since five minutes ago. Otherwise, I would say: Can the Prosecution and the Defence agree under these incidents were reported and this is the documentary evidence related to that? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to tender this one, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. That was the only reason. So I would like to tender 1D720, and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D720 receives number -- number D195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D195 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Banbury, would you please focus on paragraph 69 of your statement, and could we have P876 in e-court. P876, that is the document you discuss in paragraph 69 and 70, 71. No. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. This is document 10058, a 65 ter document under the number of 10058. 65 ter 10058. And I apologise for that error. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, you talked about this in paragraphs 69 through 71 of your statement, and I'd just like to refer you to a couple of things. The document at issue is a telegram, dispatch sent by Mr. Viktor Andreev, on the 19th of November, 1994, and in paragraph 4 of this document - could we have it, please - it is stated as follows, and I'm referring to this outgoing dispatch: "General Gobilliard presented his latest press release to Karadzic in which Gobillard condemned moderate acts made by the BH Army from within Sarajevo as well as firing of mortars by the BSA from weapons collection points as an example of UNPROFOR's neutral approach to the conflict." Now, could you please try and recall this and tell us what it was that triggered General Gobilliard's reaction and his condemnation of these particular attacks? Which events were underlying this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, drawing on the document, I think there were most likely specific incidents of firing by the BiH from within Sarajevo outside against the Serbs, and firing by the Bosnian Serb Army into Sarajevo against the BiH. I -- this was a somewhat routine occurrence. Routine is perhaps the wrong term. Frequent occurrence. And whenever -- or it would be quite normal for the United Nations following such an incident or incidents to protest to both sides, and I see this in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this at the time of the cease-fire agreement that had just been signed and that demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall a cease-fire agreement in November 1994. There was a cessation of hostilities agreement a month later in December of 1994. A lot happened between mid-November and late December in Bosnia, but in -- in this case I don't recall a cease-fire agreement, and as far as I know, there was no agreement to demilitarise Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we now see paragraph 8 of this document, please. And again I assume that you authored this telegram as indicated here. In conclusion, we see that it says: "We must pursue a concerted policy to convince the Bosnian Serb leadership that our presence is indeed in their interest and that our departure would be disastrous for them, for if they make the calculation that their interests are better served by our departure, the implications will be disastrous not only for them but also for the cause of peace in the former Yugoslavia." When you say in your conclusion "we must pursue a concerted policy," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "we" I refer to UNPROFOR, and in particular the leadership of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned demilitarisation of Sarajevo, and what I would like to ask you about is the demilitarisation of Igman, Mount Igman. Do you recall at any point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where are you referring to, demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said -- let me just check. You said, "You mentioned demilitarisation of Sarajevo," and I was wondering what you were referring to exactly, to this document or to the statement of the witness or to any other source, or did I miss ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness mentioned the demilitarisation of Sarajevo in his earlier answer, and what I said was I am not really going to refer to that but, rather, the Mount Igman demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness said, "There was no agreement to demilitarise Sarajevo." So that's clear. No -- where does he say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does he say anything about Mount Igman? I mean, is it an open question not in relation to any part of his statement or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour, although that can be found in the statement, and we'll touch upon it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But the reason I'm asking you this now is because of the following -- the document that will come next. My question is, was there any talk about the demilitarisation of Mount Igman in 1994? Were you aware of any of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there was some agreement between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian government on the -- that was facilitated by UNPROFOR calling for the demilitarisation of Mount Igman or at least parts of Mount Igman. I believe that agreement was reached shortly before my arrival in Bosnia, and I am not very familiar with the details of that agreement, but, yes, there was an agreement that the parties entered into that created -- in which they took on obligations, each of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have a look at a document. It's a 65 ter document, 1D719.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you want to tender the last one we had on our screens, Mr. Stojanovic, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. This document bears the number 10058. It's a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10058 receives number D196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D196 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two documents are related, and this might answer your previous question, Your Honours. We'll go back to this document now. So could we see D196 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the reason for which I'll be putting this question to you: The question has to do with the demilitarisation of Igman. That's the question I put to you. Please have a look at paragraph 3 of this message that you drafted, which states the following: "According to the report from the meeting, Karadzic and Tolimir pressed us hard on the continued presence of BiH in the Mount Igman area of the demilitarised zone." Could you see that sentence. I asked you about what you knew with regard to those tasks. Could we now have a look at 1D719, 1D719. And in August 1994, prior to the comments that were made by Karadzic and Tolimir, General van Baal again writes to the Brigadier-General Jovan Divjak and he says the following: "After I wrote to you on 6 August 1994 regarding the deliberate violations of the demilitarised zone on Mount Igman, I have again been informed that your soldiers are continuing to violate the agreement. In my last letter I informed you of a certain number of violations. In the meantime, five incidents have been reported to us." And then these incidents are listed. And in the last sentence of the document it says that UNPROFOR again stresses that such activities are unacceptable and represent a direct violation of the agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that on the next page or -- it seems to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's the last sentence on the next page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR reiterates that such activities are unacceptable and represent direct violations of the agreement reached with you last year." My question is whether this document has refreshed your memory about the fact that in the course of frequent contact that you had with the authorities of Republika Srpska and with the Republika Srpska Army, in the course of such meetings were such objections by the Republika Srpska often made with regard to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such objections often were made. I don't recall saying that I could not remember the Bosnian Serbs making such objections. It was rather common for the Bosnian Serb military and political authorities to object to UNPROFOR about alleged violations of various responsibilities, commitments, et cetera, by the BiH, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I apologise. I was waiting for the interpretation to finish. What I wanted to ask you about, bearing in mind everything that you testified about yesterday which I found very interesting and of much importance, concerns your interpretation of safe areas. In this situation -- in such a situation in 1994, did UNPROFOR have a mandate to demilitarise Igman?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the Igman agreement, but normally what would happen when we would facilitate negotiations between the parties on some agreement, whether it was on Mount Igman or cessation of hostilities, the agreement would contain obligations voluntarily entered into by the parties that imposed -- imposed obligations on the parties. Sorry, I'm being redundant. It would not normally be the case that UNPROFOR was responsible for ensuring or enforcing one party or the other, any party, to fulfil their obligations. Normally the UNPROFOR role would be to monitor, observe, facilitate, patrol, report, but we would not be -- we would not enter into a commitment to force the Bosnian Serbs or force the Bosnian government to fulfil their obligations. In the case of Mount Igman, the agreement, I'd really have to look at it to comment in any detail. I would also say there is a very important distinction between Security Council Resolutions and legal character of those resolutions and the obligations they commit or confer on the parties involved as compared to the -- the nature of legal obligations stemming from an agreement between two state or non-state actors. While such an agreement can confirm important obligations on such actors, they are of a very different nature than a Security Council Resolution. So for instance, it could not be the case that the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serbs would enter into an agreement that created a mandate for UNPROFOR or create obligations on us that superseded or even complemented those that were given to us by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we're dealing with the Igman area and the situation in Sarajevo, I'd like to ask you the following: Do you know, did you have any information at your post at the time according to which the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina used the Igman area to provide logistics through the supply to the 1st Corps through the ABiH in Sarajevo, and digging was done, a route was dug out in order to be able to provide liquid fuel to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm well aware of the so-called Mount Igman route which was a road over Mount Igman and down into Sarajevo that was very heavily relied upon by the Bosnian government, Bosnian military, citizens of Sarajevo to transport goods into the city and also to travel out of the city. The city was essentially cut off from resupply, and the Mount Igman route was often the only route open that would -- that was available to bring goods into the city for the Bosnian government, the Bosnian -- or the Sarajevo citizens. So, yes, that was certainly used. In terms of the digging of a fuel supply line, I'm not aware of it, but I can certainly imagine that such a fuel supply line existed. I seem to have some small recollection of hearing something to that effect, and I can certainly imagine that such a fuel line did exist, but I don't have personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document now into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D719 receives number D197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, D197 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at paragraph 79, 80, and 81 in your statement, which is P874, and let's focus on paragraph 81. I just have one question I'd like to put to you about it. Here you meaning the 12th of December, 1994, and that's what you say in paragraph 79. You mention the meeting between Mr. Andreev, General Michael Rose, Colonel Danijel, and also Krajisnik, Koljevic, Generals Gvero and Tolimir on the other side. And then on the 12th of December, 1994, this is in paragraph 81, you say that the army told the political leaders that improving relationships with UNPROFOR depend on clearing Igman and Bjelasnica. Within two days in the course of the remainder of the meeting the Bosnian Serbs expressed positions that demonstrated a unified position -- or indicating a unified leadership, in fact. And my question is: What was this about, in fact? When you use the expression "clearing Igman," are we dealing with the same problem again?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Broadly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the army made this request, when you say the military told the political leaders, do you have Mr. Gvero and Mr. Tolimir who were present at that meeting in mind?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And new could we see P876. And while waiting for it to appear on the screen, Mr. Banbury, I'd like to put a question to you in relation to your previous answer. Given your understanding of UNPROFOR's obligations and the requests that the army conveyed through Gvero and Tolimir, was it justified to request that Igman, being a demilitarised zone, should not be used to provide logistics, equipment, weapons and ammunition to the members of the warring factions, and in particular to the 1st Corps of the ABiH in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would need to refer to the Igman agreement and specifically read it to understand exactly what the obligations were on the parties and what, if anything, UNPROFOR undertook to do based on the agreement. So, I'm sorry, I don't have a good enough recollection of the specifics of that agreement in my mind to give you a good answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, if such equipment was provided as you assume, it had to go through the tunnel in order to reach Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, it would go through the tunnel, over Igman and through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And can we agree that if the Republika Srpska Army respected the terms of the agreement on demilitarisation and didn't have the possibility of controlling the situation, would we say that this would be a very frustrating experience for one of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if two parties make agreement, if one of the parties is not keeping to its commitment to the agreement, the other party will be frustrated unless we are in a very exceptional circumstance, Witness, where they were happy. But I have never seen that, at least not often in my life. It's -- it's asking for the obvious it seems. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to force an issue that seems clear. It's clear to me. Let's go back to the document we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are aware it doesn't say anything about frustration, because your question was totally hypothetical. If the one party and if the other party, of course, that is still to be established and has not been established with this witness, because he says, "I don't recall -- I have no recollection of the details of the agreement." So also for that reason, it is -- the question was not very helpful. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have a look at -- and it's in document P876, paragraph 8. Could we have a look at paragraph 8 in P876. And I'd like to remind you that this is a weekly report for the period 5 to 11 March, from the 5th to the 11th of March. You are the author of this report, and the report states the following: "General Mladic, expressing discontent over the sanctions regime imposed on the Bosnian Serbs as well as the amount of humanitarian supplies provided to them also threatened to cut off delivery of all aid to the enclaves if sanctions were not lifted and if a greater percentage of total aid delivered in Bosnia was not given to the Serbs." And then you say: "Mladic's threats for the moment are more likely a form of pressure on UNPROFOR than an expression of genuine intent given the likely reaction by the international community in the event of a total blockade of the enclaves or an effort by the BSA to expel us from them." What is the source for this part of your weekly report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my own analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you said here General Mladic expressing discontent over the sanctions regime. What is the source for that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall offhand. My expectation is that it would have come from recent -- recent as in shortly before the writing of that report, a meeting between some UNPROFOR officials and General Mladic in which he would have expressed such a sentiment. That is what I would expect it's from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you're not in a position to tell us now where you obtained this piece of information when you say that General Mladic expressed discontent over the sanctions regime imposed on the Bosnian Serbs. So was this verified?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not in a position to tell you now from where exactly General Mladic or we would have -- we and UNPROFOR would have received such an expression from General Mladic, but it is certainly the case in what was always the case for me and I think for my colleagues that if we put something in a document of that nature where we asserting a fact essentially that we had good grounds for it. So I personally have no doubt at all that he made such an expression of sentiment, but I cannot tell you exactly where or when that took place, but I would think it was shortly before that in a meeting with the UN is my guess. I think it's highly likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, as I told you before, I would need a few minutes. Perhaps this would be a good moment to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. You will have a break of 20, 25 minutes approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to deliver additional guidance from the Chamber on timing of sending of exhibit lists and additions to exhibit lists. On the 24th of January, the Defence requested clarification with respect to the notice period for addition of new documents to proposed lists of exhibits to be used with the witness prior to the witness's testimony in court. This can be found on transcript pages 7281 through 7286. At the outset, the Chamber recalls its previous guidance of the 4th of September of 2012, transcript page 2160, in which it set out the approach to be taken with regard to this issue. In the guidance, the Chamber encouraged the parties to send such lists as early as possible and stated that it expected the first list to be sent no later than seven days prior to the witness's testimony. This list could be complemented at a later stage following any proofing of the witness. This Chamber considers that it cannot set any strict time limits for when the last documents should be added to the list of exhibits since any decision by the Chamber on this would primarily depend on the burden this addition creates on the other party. For few and short documents, a relatively short time could be sufficient. The same could apply to certain types of documents, for example, maps and/or photographs. For a large number of documents or documents of a complex nature, a longer time period would be required. The Chamber examines this on a case-by-case basis. It is for the opposing party to make a showing of prejudice due to the late filing or late notice of additions to the list of exhibits and to request a remedy. This remedy could include barring the documents could be used with a particular witness, the possibility of recalling the witness, or the postponement of the witness's testimony. In this regard, the Chamber invites the parties to first try to get any necessary clarification from each other and resolve the issue, and only if no agreement can be reached seize the Chamber of the matter. And this concludes the Chamber's additional guidance on this matter. We take a break, and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Stojanovic, the late start after the break was not due to the Chamber. We've been waiting there for ten minutes. You have until quarter past 1.00 to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly on the matter the Chamber inquired about, our position with respect to when we could file a response. We would be unable to file a response until next Wednesday. Given that it has some consequences for today, the Prosecution would have no objection to the time for the Defence to file their 94 bis filing until the Chamber would decide after -- decide the issue after seeing our submission next Wednesday, if that's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, we're still on the same subject. Could we have P876 on our monitors, please, and I'd like to refer you to paragraph 13. And I will have a few questions about that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Stojanovic. We do not receive translation at this moment. Could you please restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this paragraph reads as follows: The international peace effort to resolve the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina appears to be stalled with the contact group largely in disarray following its fragmentation into three informal though separate blocks, each with its own agenda. And then you go on to describe this further. You cite the then defence minister, US Defence -- Secretary of Defence, Mr. Perry. You cite him as saying that: I don't not see prospects of a near term political solution but then he -- and our present policies are not satisfying but the alternative choice would be worse. So my question is this: This told peace effort that you described in paragraph 13, would that have a reflection or an impact on the agreements that would be reached in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually there was -- excuse me. Usually there was an inverse relationship between the strength of the peace process and the strength of the -- or the activity of the military effort by the parties in Bosnia. When the peace process was going well, the military activity tended to be less. When the peace process was stalled or going poorly, usually the military activity was greater, and one or the other or all sides tended to pursue their objectives through military means when they were not able to achieve progress through political means. And I think in this case that would have applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind that you mention a number of documents here, at that point in time in whose favour would a cessation of hostilities and a cease-fire be in March 1995 in other words?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that question to be properly answered by me would need additional information. The -- just the cessation of hostility, it would depend what other aspects went along with the agreement, if any. So it's very hard for me to answer that, though I would say that I think by March of 1995, the Bosnian Serbs had recognised that they were very unlikely to meet what they defined as their minimal political objectives through political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the territory that was held by the BH Army and the HVO on the one hand and the RS on the other, in the negotiation and contacts, in all of these negotiations and contacts was it the Serb side that was in favour of a cessation of hostilities on all sides? Would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, I don't believe that would be correct. I think it would be correct to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any problem. As usual, 30 seconds. We'll first wait for the witness to answer the question, and then you have 30 seconds to consult at low voice with Mr. Mladic. Could you first finish your -- Mr. Stojanovic, it would not -- I would listen to the answer of the witness first before you consult with your client. Mr. Mladic, please be seated. You will have 30 seconds after the witness has finished his answer. Would you please complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Bosnian Serb side regularly thought the conflict asserted its interest in and I referred to this yesterday, I believe, regularly asserted its interest in a peace agreement in cessation of hostilities and cease-fire, but would as a matter of course attach conditions to the peace or the cessation of hostilities that they were interested in and those conditions were invariably unacceptable to not only the Bosnian government but usually key members of the international community, states, government that were trying to promote a solution. So I think it's incorrect to say that the Bosnian Serbs wanted -- it's misleading at least to say the Bosnian Serbs wanted peace. They wanted peace but only on their terms and those terms were unacceptable to -- to many others whose agreement would be necessary for such a peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you have 30 seconds to consult with your client. And low voice, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now pull up in e-court 65 ter 10593.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that's the document you discussed in paragraph 99, 100 and 109 of your -- and 101 of your statement. And could we focus on paragraph 7 of this document. This is a weekly report sent by you covering the period 12th through 18th March 1995. Among other things, it states the blue routes across Sarajevo airport were closed on the 12th of March at the insistence of the Bosnian Serbs following the sniping deaths of two girls aged 9 and 10 in Grbavica in Serb-held Sarajevo. Did you have any information about what had actually happened and what was the reason for this kind of decision by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- well, because the report I wrote indicates that these two girls were killed by sniping, I have no doubt at all that it's true that two young Serb girls were in a very horrible way killed by sniping, in this case by the Bosnian government -- or Bosnian government soldier. So at that clearly happened in my view. The response of the Serbs, they had different responses at different times to sniping by Bosnian Army forces. At this period of time, they were saying that for every Serb civilian or at least Serb person killed by sniping, then they would respond by shutting the blue routes across the airport, that were critical to allowing large numbers of civilians from both sides, though more from the Bosnian government side, to travel in and out of Sarajevo. They would close these routes for 30 days for each person killed by Bosnian government or Bosnian Army forces by sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will move on to the next document. I do not intend to tender this one, Your Honour, because I've quoted the paragraph that I was concerned with. Could we now have 65 ter 10597.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's another weekly report covering the period -- or actually dated the 15th of April, 1995. I would like to focus on paragraph 1, in which you state in this report, that's paragraph 1 on the next page, thank you. And it says there: "A French soldier was killed by sniping in Dobrinja on 14 April while standing in his light armoured vehicle. On 15 April, another French soldier was killed by sniping while erecting an anti-sniping barricade on snipers' alley. An investigation of the first incident has so far proven inconclusive, and it is unlikely that evidence will be sufficient to attribute responsibility for the murder." And my question is this: Do you know whether after the drafting of this report it was established who shot this French soldier?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I do no. I certainly do not recollect at this time. I don't know if I ever knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to briefly move to another document and we'll return to this one. Could we see 65 ter 1D712. I wanted to discuss this document together with you. It's dated the 22nd of April, 1995. It is addressed to army General Rasim Delic, the general of the BH Army, by the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you. I believe there is an English version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, your microphone was not activated. There is no English version in e-court if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On your list for the cross-examination, its even indicated that there is only an original and not translation, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. We have agreed to submit a request for an official translation, but with your leave I will read the document, and then I will tender it for identification purposes alone pending an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I'm looking at Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was trying to determine whether we've done translations through the booths in this manner. I certainly don't oppose the process, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course the booth, our interpreters are not there to translate, that is to -- but if you slowly read the relevant portion of this document, which seems to be a document coming from Alija Izetbegovic, dated the 21st of April, 1995. So it's two documents. It's two documents, as a matter of fact. We have the document on our screen consists of two documents, it seems. The upper part, 22nd of April, 1995; the lower part 21st of April, 1995. The lower part apparently coming from the BiH republic and then the Presidency, I take it, and the upper parts seems to be more of a military document. From which part are you going to read, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second part, Your Honour, dated the 21st of April, 1995. Where the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina writes to General Delic, the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army. I will try to pace myself. Thank you. Alija Izetbegovic in this document says to the commander, Commander Delic, the following: "General, this morning the French ambassador Henri Zakolen visited me in my office and told my counsellor, Memija, among other things the following: The official France is very angry because of the murder of its soldier in Dobrinja. Military expertise shows that the soldier was shot from a position under the control of the Bosnian Army, but we cannot verify that which gives rise to suspicions. The Chetniks have been extremely co-operative in this case, allowing UN investigators to enter every apartment and to have access to every position along their line."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you at this moment. [Microphone not activated] ... I wonder what we expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I'm not being heard either. You were just not heard or recorded on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then try to repeat what I said. I think my microphone was activated but there seemed to be some practical problem.
