Mr. Stojanovic, the witness told us that he already at that time reported that they could not attribute responsibility. If this is about the first one, is it? If so, then of course it's not of great use to put to the witness what others may have said about it unless you would expect him to have any specific knowledge about what others may have found or may not have found or written down. So would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour. And if you allow me, the next sentence will actually be my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The document -- this document further reads as follows: "The French ambassador took a soft guard when he claimed that he had evidence that of the 24 of their soldiers, members of the UN, who were killed not counting those who were killed in a car accident on Igman, more than half of these were committed by the BH Army. Now, the question is this: During your mission, did you receive information to the same effect in this period?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a very specific matter that half or more than half of the French soldiers killed in other than a car accident, they were killed by Bosnian Army actions, I do not have that specific information. As a more general matter, there were very often claims made either by the Bosnian Serbs or by UNPROFOR officials that UNPROFOR personnel had been targeted by Bosnian Army personnel. In -- according to my knowledge, in a rather small portion of those cases was it proven that the attack had come from the Bosnian Army, but it is certainly the case that some attacks against UNPROFOR, shootings or other incidents, were originated by Bosnian Army forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. You said: In a rather small portion of those cases was it proved that the attack had come from the Bosnian Army, but it is certainly the case that some attacks against UNPROFOR shootings originated by Bosnian Army forces. It looks as if you're making a distinction between two or were you just repeating what you said? It's Bosnian Army twice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour, for the lack of clarity. I was repeating essentially the same point that while there was a very small portion, certainly some attacks had come from the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, at this point I'd like to tender this document, 1D712 for identification pending a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D712 receives number D198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to refer you to your statement. That's P874, specifically paragraph 120, which discusses this particular document, and what I would like to ask you is this: Are you aware that at this time there was intense sniping from positions held by the BH Army and that this was an ongoing complaint by the VRS authorities?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sniping was a very recurring problem by both sides including the Bosnian Army, and I'm not a hundred per cent certain at this specific time that there was a high rate of sniping incidents, but I can certainly anticipate that having been the case and we -- we did face problems with Bosnian government forces sniping, whether it's a 9-year-old girl or a 10-year-old girl or an older woman. There were terrible incidents involving sniping against Serb civilians that UNPROFOR worked very hard to combat and stop and follow up on, as we did on all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, your reference to P874 must have been mistake. The statement is P876. I don't know whether it's a translation error or anything else, but let's proceed. It is the correct number. Yes. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us return to your statement, and we have it in e-court, and I would like to refer you to paragraph 153 of your statement. So this would be P876.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is P874.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, I made a mistake when correcting you. I apologised for that, but we are with your statement in P874. I might have seduced you to make a similar mistake as I did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So let us take a look at paragraph 153, and this because I would like to mention a document related to that. Here we have an interpretation and your comments on the minutes of a meeting attended by Mr. Karadzic that was held on the 30th of April, 1995. That you can see in paragraph 145 of your statement, but what I would like to ask you about is this: You mentioned there and said that Karadzic told all those seated at the table that the Serbs did not wish to dominate over the Muslims but, rather, it is the Muslims who want to dominate the Serbs. And he said, "We have lived with the Muslims for 500 years." The same situation can be seen in Cyprus and so on, but this is what I would like to ask you: Are you aware whether Mr. Karadzic ever said something like that, and so that you have knowledge about it, but on the basis of what was it that he claimed that at that point in time the Muslims wanted to dominate the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did he ever make any reference to why it was that he was claiming that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall a specific reference by Dr. Karadzic as to why he held that belief. He certainly made many complaints or observations about the behaviour or intentions of the Bosnian Muslim community and political structure, but do I not recall a specific reference he made as to why he held that belief at that time. I do know that at that time in Bosnia the cessation of hostilities agreement that had been negotiated with the assistance of President Carter had essentially collapsed and the political process was in a very bad state and there was heightened military activity, heightened isolation of the Bosnian Serbs in Pale, whether it was from Belgrade or Moscow or the strengthening of the federation. And there was military activity on the ground that was perhaps not going in the favour of the Bosnian Serbs and probably some more strengthening including through external arm shipments of the federation armies. So at that particular time, I think one could understand if the Bosnian Serbs felt as if things were not going their way and they were under more and more pressure politically and militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you this question, because I would like us to have a look at 1D710. 1D710. And I would like us to comment on it. Your Honours, this is the transcript of the minutes of a meeting held on the 29th of April, 1995, one day earlier. The meeting was held in the cabinet of the president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman. The meeting was attended on behalf of the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ejup Ganic, Muhamed Sacirbey and Kasim Trnka; Mr. Tudjman was also present and Mr. Sanader and Mr. Radin. At this meeting they discussed the situation and the relationship of Croatia with the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could we now have a look at pages 23 and 24 in the B/C/S version and I've been told its page 3 and 4 in the English version because only the part that I'm interested in, the part that I want to use, has been translated. And, Your Honours, this translation is the Defence's unofficial translation. The discussion between the individuals I have just mentioned, Mr. Banbury, at one point in time Mr. Tudjman said -- and this is noted in the margin. Could we see please see the following page in the English version. He says: "Look, either we will create this federation, because if what we have agreed in isn't pursued, then we won't leave those Croatian parts." And then Ejup Ganic replies: "Mr. President, perhaps I'm not being realistic, but I think that strengthening the federation Serbian entity would be marginalised. Do you understand me?" Tudjman says: "It's understandable." And then Ejup Ganic says: "We have to unite militarily but officially pretend to be mad. We have to unite. We need to arm ourselves better. Why are you imposing restrictions on us in that respect?" And he says: "We know what the world will allow us. We can put the Serbs in Bosnia in a marginal position." These are things that Mr. Karadzic said on that occasion and you referred to that in paragraph 143 of your statement. Was it that the Serbs didn't want to dominate the Muslims? Is that what is said? Was it said that it is the Muslims who want to dominate the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never seen this document before, but I find it to be very consistent with remarks I made a moment ago about the increasing isolation of the Bosnian Serbs, the strengthening of the federation militarily and politically, including through perhaps increased arms shipments, and hence it would be understandable if the Bosnian Serb leadership at this time felt under increasing political and military pressure and greater isolation. I do not take away from this document either that the Bosnian Serbs did not want to dominate the Muslims nor do I take away from Dr. Karadzic's statement that -- I do not necessarily believe that because he said it, it meant it was true. And at the same time I do not take away from this document that the Bosnian government or the federation wanted to dominate the Serbs. I think there are important distinctions between the -- the Republika Srpska and the Serb people, and I think there is a big difference between seeking to marginalise or weaken an enemy against whom one is fighting and what the future intentions might be in terms of treatment of populations, majority, minority, or plurality and minority in a future political entity in a peace agreement. So I think it's one -- I'm reluctant to generalise along the lines that you've suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, may I ask you what you exactly asked, because what you said, you are referring to a meeting on which reports were written by the witness about what Mr. Karadzic said, and then you come up with the minutes of another meeting, and then your question was: Was it that the Serbs didn't want to dominate the Muslims? Is that what is said? Was it said that it is the Muslims who want to dominate the Serbs? Now, that's clear, because in the report we find what Mr. Karadzic said, and it's exactly what you quoted. Now, may I take it that your answer was whether what was said during the meet with the Croatian president, whether that is consistent with what was said by Mr. Karadzic? Was that your question? Because I'm totally lost, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in fact my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you didn't phrase it like that, but apparently that's what you wanted to ask the witness. The witness told us some of his thoughts on the matter. Would you agree with me and perhaps we could ask the witness that what was said during the meeting in the -- with the president of Croatia that that was about the federation who was fighting against Serbs and was not specifically about Muslims as a group, but that the Muslims together with Croats would marginalise the Serbs. I'm asking myself to what extent a general sweeping statement on Muslims always wanting to dominate and then to refer to certain countries where this happened how that -- do we have to understand that to be the same as the Muslims making an affiliation with another people or nation, whatever you would like to call it, the Croats, and then to fight against the Serbs? It's unclear to me, but I do not know, Witness, apparently you have understood what the question was. I had difficulties understanding it. But was that one of the differences you pointed at when you gave your -- could I say little speech rather than an answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was one the points that I had sought to make, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then that is at least clear. Could you try to formulate your questions in such a way that they are understood well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to tender this document into evidence. At the moment, it's marked as a 65 ter document, 1D710.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the recording in the transcript of the conversation with the Croatian president. Ms. Bibles, do you have no objections? What I see -- yes, not -- not to be MFI'd [microphone not activated] of apparently a large document where small portions are taken out which I think -- has the whole of the document been disclosed to the Prosecution or is it your document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It was originally, I believe, a document seized by the OTP, Your Honour, or taken by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber, however -- if there is a more full translation of it, then of course the Chamber would like to have a possibility to look at the context of the excerpts that are presented in this document. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D710 receives number 1D -- the number D199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D199 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banbury. You mentioned the tunnel on a number of occasions and I would like to ask you something about that. Were you familiar with this manner of providing Sarajevo with supplies? Did you have any personal experience of this manner of providing Sarajevo with supplies?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was well aware of the existence of the tunnel and the manner of supplying Sarajevo with supplies using it. I never personally observed any physical aspect of the tunnel, the entrance to the tunnel, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information according to which in addition to military equipment, narcotics, tobacco, goods of a general kind were provided, goods that could be used on the black market or sold on the black market?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my understanding that all manner of goods were transported in and out of the tunnel, well, particularly through the tunnel to Sarajevo. To the extent that they showed up on a so-called black market, I don't know what arrangements the Bosnian government may have had, but I assumed they controlled the tunnel very well, which meant they must have approved the supplies going through it. So if the government approved it, I don't think it means they would end up on a black market. So -- but there were certainly commercial goods going in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us given the work you did which units of the ABiH had control over that feature, which particular unit had control?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was never much of an expert on military units and which units on either side were deployed in which area, so I cannot tell you the -- the answer to that question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we have another look at paragraph 180 of your statement, Exhibit P874. I just have one question about this part of your statement. It's the 10th of July, 1995. That's the date. It concerns the situation around Srebrenica. And you say that evening, on 10th of July, the commander of UNPROFOR, Janvier, spoke to General Tolimir and suggested that he establish a cease-fire. Tolimir said that he issued an order -- that he had issued an order for a cease-fire. Did General Tolimir -- or, rather, was General Tolimir at the time a person who was in the position to issue an order of this kind for a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question. It's possible that on July 10th when that conversation took place UNPROFOR, including myself, would have thought he would be in a position because we did not know the enormity of the military undertaking that had been initiated by the Bosnian Serbs. Instead, we at the time may have thought it was a localised skirmish, a routine kind of, you know, probing attack that we had seen on many other occasions which could be stopped by General Tolimir given his position. In retrospect, knowing what we know now, I don't believe he would have been in a position to give that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I have limited time, I just have another question. You said that Tolimir said that he had issued an order for a cease-fire. I'm only asking you whether you stand by that claim. According to the information you had, did he in fact say that he had issued an order to establish the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I read stop the firing, not cease-fire which are two different concepts. Cease-fire includes two parties. Stop firing can be done one-sidedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could answer the question now then whether Tolimir said that he gave an order to stop firing, whether that's what you heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I certainly stand by the representation in the paragraph that General Tolimir told General Janvier that he, General Tolimir, had issued an order to the Serb forces to stop firing, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we are close to the point where you're expected to conclude. If you have one or more -- two -- a few more questions, then I'll give you another three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to draw attention to paragraph 183, 185, and 186 of your statement which refer to your meeting with General Mladic in Mali Zvornik on the 1st of September, 1995. What interests me in relation to this meeting that you described in detail is whether you remember whether at that time the French pilots whose planes were shot down above Republika Srpska were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first -- you have an opportunity to consult with Mr. Mladic, and then we'll see whether after the break there's any additional question. Could you first please finish your question. We'll hear the answer from the witness, and then we'll take the break. Mr. Mladic, please be seated for the next one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- if you'd like me to respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps what Mr. Stojanovic said is that he was interested in the relation between the meeting you have described at the time and whether the French pilots whose planes were shot down were discussed. Was it your question whether that incident was discussed at this meeting? Was that the question, Mr. Stojanovic? Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- to be certain, I would prefer to refer to my notes, but it's my recollection that I believe they were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I suggest -- Ms. Bibles, how much time would you need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Very little time, Your Honour, if any five minutes at this moment at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest the following: We take a break now. You'll have a possibility to consult with Mr. Mladic during the break. We will resume at 20 minutes to 2.00, and you'll then have, I would say, another 15 minutes at the maximum so that there will be sufficient time for Ms. Bibles for any re-examination. We'll proceed in that way. We'll take a break. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'd like to inform the parties that the matter we discussed this morning in private session, the decision on the motion involved, has been made and will be communicated to you by e-mail within the next half an hour or perhaps it may even already be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you remember, before the break we were dealing with the analysis of a meeting in Mali Zvornik on the 1st of September, 1995. Would you agree with me that that was a period of intense NATO aircraft overflights; at the time NATO planes were flying over the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about two French pilots, and I asked you whether they were discussed at the meeting, and you say that you believe so but that you would like to consult your notes. To the best of your recollection, could you tell the Chamber the nature of the discussion concerning the French pilots? Could you tell the Chamber something about the discussion about the pilots?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two French pilots were being held by the Bosnian Serb forces and there was a strong desire and effort by UNPROFOR and the French contingent in UNPROFOR and certainly been the French authorities to gain the release of the pilots. The objective was simply to get the pilots released by the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware at one point in time these French pilots were released.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where this happened, and do you know who handed over the pilots in question and to whom?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not recall the specifics. I probably have a record of it somewhere, but I don't recall myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it refresh your memory if I said that the French Ministry of Defence participated in these discussions that related to handing over the French pilots to the French authorities? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is consistent with my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any dispute about these matters, for example? Is there any dispute between the parties on -- I mean the witness is kind enough to answer the questions, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's not even sure how this would be necessary or relevant to an adjudication of the indictment, but again I'm reluctant to make agreements off the top of my head, but I'm happy to discuss with Defence any possible agreement on facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it has been not explored. Therefore, Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will then ask you if it would refresh your memory if I said that this hand-over of the wounded French pilots, the pilots whose wounds were treated, took place in the municipality of Zvornik in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly believe that to be the case. I again don't recall specifically, but that seems entirely plausible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And given the fact that we intend to call them as witnesses, I would like to ask you whether you have noted down any information on these pilots, their first and last names and other personal details that concern them?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall having done so. It's possible. I have some -- some record of personal details in my notes on the pilots. I think it's somewhat unlikely though, but the fact that they had been shot down, taken captive, held, released, I would have some of that information in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Given that in the summary of your statement, which has been admitted or will be admitted into evidence, there's nothing about those discussions held on the 1st of September 1995 about that subject that was discussed there. So is there a reason for which you didn't answer those questions, or did the Prosecution not put any questions to you that concerned the situation that the pilots were in?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly would have tried to answer any questions to the best of my ability, and I'm sure that if the issue were discussed or to the extent it was discussed in the September 1 meeting in Mali Zvornik, I would have taken notes of that and those discussions would be reflected in the notes that I have. But not -- my -- my notes are voluminous and my statement is a very short abridged summary of some aspects of them, so not everything in my notes of course appears in the -- my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I ask you to comment on paragraph 187 of your statement, P874. I apologise. Paragraph 188. At one point in time General Mladic left the meeting. He protested because there were NATO aircraft overflying the territory of Republika Srpska right up until the end of that meeting. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And four hours later, the meeting resumed after General Mladic's proposals were accepted relating to the NATO overflights that should stop pending this resolution.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I think there may have been a slight adjustment to the final arrangement. The final arrangement was slightly different perhaps than what General Mladic had proposed, but broadly speaking those were the conditions under which the meeting recommenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And at this continuation of the meeting, in view of what you said in paragraph 188 of your statement, General Mladic raised the issue, among other things, why his proposal was not accepted, the proposal relating to the establishment of a joint commission after Markale II incident. Do you recall that question of his, and did any -- did Mr. Janvier offer any response to that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that issue, and while I am not certain what General Janvier's response was, I know the UNPROFOR position on that issue which I would anticipate General Janvier would have communicated at the time, and the UNPROFOR position was that we had done an investigation using competent professionals to conduct it, and we were satisfied with the results and we found the results to be conclusive. So there was no need from the UNPROFOR perspective to pursue any further investigation. The results to us were clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the use of NATO -- the NATO Air Force come upon a request of General Smith, and is it true that Mr. Gobillard was not at that point in time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that the use of NATO airpower following that Markale incident in August 1995 came at the request of General Smith. Your question -- on the transcript it says "Janvier" I heard "Gobillard." Smith was Gobillard's superior officer so his presence would not have mattered but it is true that General Janvier was outside of the UNPROFOR area of operations and hence not in a position to call or not call for NATO air support at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a transcript problem on page 68 in line 9. My question related to General Janvier, so my question was whether General Janvier was at that point in time when the NATO aviation was called, whether he was in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the matter was resolved already, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I failed to see the reply, because I know that Gobillard was mentioned, but my question was whether Janvier was there because this meeting was on the 1st of September, in other words three days after the events surrounding Markale II.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel please repeat the last portion of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the witness told us is that he heard the name Gobillard mentioned, but that he took it that the question was about Janvier and then he -- he responded -- he has answered that question as if it had been about the presence of General Janvier being away, General Janvier being away. So the matter has been resolved. Mr. Stojanovic, it's about time, I think, to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have a few more questions and I will stick to the 15 minutes that were agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have used approximately your 15 minutes. You can put one or two more questions and also in view of the matters you raised, Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber is not inclined to give you more time than we have done already. Let's say two more questions and then it's time for Ms. Bibles to further examine the witness if she has any need. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you could we see in e-court P874, paragraph 161. This is May 1995, Mr. Banbury. You talk about the notes that you took when you accompanied Mr. Akashi at his meeting with Mr. Milosevic, and you say that he said, among other things, and that's in paragraph 161: I will get in touch with Mladic and then -- and convince him to meet with Smith to resolve this issue, these banality. It's like a child's game. He's an honest man, you know. He has some problems with his political leadership, but if Karadzic finds out he'll exploit it and say he's under my influence. Now, I'd like to ask you this: While you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when you had all these meetings with Mr. Mladic and contacts with various political and military leaders, was this position on General Mladic, the position that you described yesterday during the examination-in-chief, was that position something that you yourself also took?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand precisely the question. Which position was -- are you asking if I took?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please rephrase the question, Mr. Stojanovic. Make it a clear question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This phrase that General Mladic was an honest man, was that something that was always present in the background in people's minds in all these meetings that you attended? Did you actually hear a similar assessment of General Mladic from Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought that this is what Mr. Milosevic had said. This is the -- what Mr. Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic is reported to have said that he considered Mr. Mladic to be an honest man. So now to ask this witness: Did you actually hear a similar assessment of General Mladic from Mr. Milosevic. Do you intend to say that at any other occasion Mr. Milosevic had said the same or is it that other people would have said the same about Mr. Mladic? What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The latter, sir. Is -- did you hear a similar assessment of General Mladic from other people as well?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear other Bosnian Serb officials characterise General Mladic's character. I did hear very often, in participating conversations, very often with senior UNPROFOR officials and it was I think the widely held view among UNPROFOR people who dealt with General Mladic that he very often misrepresented the truth to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. Bibles, any questions in re-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No questions for re-examination of this witness, Your Honour. We do have 12 associated exhibits to deal with later but I don't believe we need the witness for those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see whether my colleagues or I have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no further questions. We don't need the witness for the associated exhibits, which means that, Mr. Banbury, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for come to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, which are the remaining -- which are the remaining associated exhibits to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could begin with 09738, which was introduced by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: This is one we initially indicated that we would not tender. However, the Defence did introduce this on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Document 09738 receives number P877, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10595 receives number P881, Your Honours.

utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, P885, Madam Registrar, is admitted under that number. I see you are agreeing with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, admitted into evidence. Are there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On page 74, line 13, it should read "P886."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P886 and it was admitted, and P886 relates to 65 ter 10654. Any other matter to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
